title: Alleged victim speaks out after former Coffee Co. deputy accused of tracking her is released on bond

reading.body:
This is an alleged misuse of access, not a model failure. A person with legitimate credentials is accused of querying law enforcement systems, a camera network and a tag reader network, for a purpose those systems were not built to serve. The systems performed as designed and returned the data they were asked for, which is why no technical control inside them would have flagged the queries as wrong.

The failure sits at the point of authorised access, where the only check on a query is the intent of the person making it. Catching it would have required an audit of query logs against stated case purposes, or a supervisor reviewing lookups that had no investigative justification. The reporting does not say whether any such logging or review existed.

An indictment is an allegation, not a finding of guilt, and the outcome of the case is not established. The reporting does not establish how the tracking was discovered, what the eight counts individually allege, or whether the systems involved had any monitoring at the time.

reports.title: Alleged victim speaks out after former Coffee Co. deputy accused of tracking her is released on bond

summary:
A former Coffee County deputy, Chris Ashley Rozar, was released on bond after a grand jury indicted him on eight counts, including stalking and misusing law enforcement databases. The 49-year-old is accused of using the sheriff's office camera system, tag reader system, and a state crime database for personal reasons between April and May 2024. He was terminated when the investigation began and was arrested on May 5.

The woman he allegedly tracked spoke anonymously, saying she waited two years for the investigation and hopes her story helps other women report abuse. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation led the case after the former sheriff requested an independent review. Rozar is scheduled for arraignment on May 27 in Coffee County Superior Court.
